title: Flattened Matrix Search: When to Use It

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only matrix-binary-search program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Treat the 3×4 sample as a single sorted array of length 12. Flat index i maps to row i/4 and column i%4. Search for 16 returns true; individually sorted rows without global row-major order would not suffice.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return true when 16 is present. The visible fixture is `[[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]]` and its example result is `true`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Flattened Matrix Search when it asks for sorted rectangular matrices. Here the concrete task is: Return true when 16 is present. The visible input `[[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. It needs ordering, a monotone predicate, or another proved structure that lets one half be discarded; merely containing numbers is not enough. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Map a flat midpoint back to row and column when rows form one global sorted order. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? Binary search maintains an interval that is still capable of containing the answer. State precisely why the discarded half cannot contain it. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(log(rows*cols)) time · O(1) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `true` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check no match, duplicate matches, the first and last valid positions, and an answer at the boundary of the search domain. Use half-open bounds consistently and compute the midpoint without overflowing large integer indices. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
